distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer disease leaf for acute inflammation/infection centered on colonic diverticula. Uncomplicated, complicated, perforated, abscess-forming, fistulizing, right-sided, sigmoid, multifocal, elderly, young, recurrent, and immunocompromised contexts remain axes, risk modifiers, source-control states, or future subtype layers rather than disease-name qualifiers.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking may consume pain location, tenderness, fever or blunted fever, bowel-habit symptoms, inflammatory labs, and presentation imaging such as diverticula, focal colonic wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, pericolic gas, abscess, or peritonitis. Final paper diagnosis, operative pathology, colonoscopy performed only to adjudicate malignancy/IBD, treatment response, and follow-up outcome should stay confirmatory/non-ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly includes them.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Pre-existing colonic diverticula in a susceptible segment, most often sigmoid/left colon but also right colon, cecum, hepatic flexure, transverse colon, or multifocal disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Diverticular neck obstruction and mucosal microinjury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Fecalith or inspissated stool, dysmotility, luminal pressure, and focal mucosal injury obstruct a diverticular neck and initiate localized bacterial overgrowth, ischemic stress, and microperforation.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Colonic gram-negative and anaerobic microbial burden
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Localized contamination by colonic flora, including Enterobacterales and anaerobes, sustains inflammation after microperforation or abscess formation until containment, active antimicrobial coverage, or source control changes the vector field.
Neutrophil, macrophage, cytokine, edema, and fat inflammation around the inflamed diverticulum produce focal pain, tenderness, bowel-habit changes, mural thickening, and pericolic fat stranding.

Small extraluminal gas, localized mesocolic fluid, phlegmon, or abscess reflect perforation walled off by mesentery or omentum. This raises complication and source-control need without automatically implying generalized peritonitis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Free perforation and generalized peritonitis transition
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Failure of local containment allows purulent or feculent contamination of the peritoneal cavity, producing diffuse peritonitis, pneumoperitoneum, shock physiology, emergency source-control need, and high mortality hazard.

Local colonic inflammation, abscess, or perforation drives fever, chills, leukocytosis, CRP/procalcitonin rise, tachycardia, lactate, AKI hazard, and shock hazard; older or immunosuppressed hosts may show blunted fever or WBC response.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Active coverage, containment, and recovery capacity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Effective conservative management, adequate antimicrobial coverage when needed, drainage or surgery when source control is required, symptom control, and host reserve reshape the disease trajectory toward resolution.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Acute diverticulitis requires diverticula in the involved segment.
Sigmoid involvement is common in many Western presentations.
Right-sided diverticula can be the substrate for cecal, ascending, hepatic-flexure, or transverse diverticulitis.
Obstruction and microinjury create a local contaminated compartment.
Colonic flora drive local innate inflammation.
The inflamed diverticulum is the focal lesion.
Mural edema and inflammation thicken the involved colonic segment.
Inflamed pericolic fat stranding is a core CT signal.
Pericolic inflammation produces localized abdominal pain.
Sigmoid or descending disease classically produces LLQ pain.
Cecal or ascending diverticulitis can mimic appendicitis with RLQ pain.
Hepatic-flexure or proximal transverse disease can present with RUQ or upper abdominal pain.
Tenderness localizes over the inflamed segment.
Visceral inflammation and ileus physiology can produce nausea or vomiting.
Acute abdominal inflammation commonly reduces appetite or oral intake.
Local edema, pain, diet change, and slowed motility can reduce stool output.
Some cases present with diarrhea, especially more extensive colonic inflammation.
Contained microperforation is observed as localized pericolic gas or fluid.
Small locules of gas adjacent to the colon mark contained perforation.
Persistent localized contamination can organize into an abscess.
Abscess, fistula, obstruction, or uncontrolled perforation may require drainage or surgery.
Free perforation can release intraperitoneal air.
Failure of containment raises macroscopic GI perforation risk.
Purulent or feculent contamination produces generalized peritonitis.
Generalized peritonitis is a procedural source-control state.
Free contamination can precipitate septic shock.
Fever is common but may be absent in older or immunosuppressed patients.
Measured temperature may be high, normal, or blunted.
Chills or rigors can accompany febrile bacterial inflammation.
Pain, fever, dehydration, and systemic inflammation raise pulse.
Leukocytosis is common in acute diverticulitis.
Bacterial colonic inflammation often produces neutrophil predominance.
CRP tracks acute colonic inflammation and severity.
Shock or hypoperfusion raises lactate.
Sepsis, dehydration, and contrast/procedural contexts can precipitate AKI.
Active coverage and containment reduce viable local microbial burden.
Adequate drainage, surgery, or containment lowers uncontrolled source activity.
Systemic inflammation, shock, organ dysfunction, perforation, and failed source control drive near-term mortality.
Generalized peritonitis carries substantially higher death risk than contained disease.

axes.shape_free_text: Presence of one or more colonic diverticula.
Focal inflamed diverticulum or diverticulum-centered inflammatory segment.
Focal or segmental colonic mural thickening centered on the involved diverticular segment.
Pericolic or mesenteric fat stranding adjacent to the inflamed diverticular segment.
Small locules of extraluminal gas adjacent to the inflamed colon, suggesting contained perforation or microperforation.
Contained microperforation with localized pericolic gas, mesocolic fluid, or limited phlegmon without generalized peritonitis.
Free intraperitoneal air away from the inflamed segment, concerning for free perforation when not explained by recent procedure.
Pericolic, pelvic, mesocolic, retroperitoneal, or distant abscess related to diverticular perforation.
Inflamed diverticular segment involves sigmoid colon.
Inflamed segment involves cecum, ascending colon, hepatic flexure, or proximal transverse colon.
Inflamed diverticular segment involves cecum.
Inflamed diverticular segment involves hepatic flexure or adjacent proximal transverse colon.
Two or more separated inflamed diverticular colonic regions during the same episode.
Abdominal pain from inflamed diverticular segment; location depends on involved colon.
LLQ pain, typical of sigmoid or descending colonic diverticulitis.
RLQ pain from cecal or ascending diverticulitis; overlaps appendicitis mimic space.
RUQ pain from hepatic-flexure or proximal transverse diverticulitis; overlaps gallbladder, liver abscess, and biliary mimic space.
Epigastric pain radiating to the back; uncommon in diverticulitis but can appear with proximal transverse/hepatic-flexure disease and remains a pancreatitis mimic axis.
Focal or diffuse abdominal tenderness over the involved diverticular segment.
Rebound, guarding, rigidity, or peritoneal irritation; diffuse signs raise free perforation/source-control need.
Nausea, vomiting, or retching during acute diverticulitis or ileus-like visceral inflammation.
Anorexia, poor appetite, reduced intake, or food avoidance during acute abdominal illness.
Constipation, decreased stool content, or reduced stool output during diverticulitis.
Diarrhea, loose stools, or frequent slimy stools; overlaps colitis mimics and antibiotic exposure.
Subjective or documented fever history.
Measured temperature; can be febrile, normal, or blunted.
Chills, rigors, sweats, or systemic febrile discomfort accompanying acute diverticular inflammation.
Heart rate during presentation; pain, fever, dehydration, or sepsis can raise it.
Respiratory rate; severe pain, fever, acidosis, or shock can raise it.
Systolic blood pressure; may be preserved or low with sepsis, dehydration, or free perforation.
MAP; low values mark shock physiology and outcome hazard.
Oxygen saturation; usually normal unless severe sepsis, aspiration, atelectasis, or comorbidity is present.
Peripheral WBC count; often elevated but can be normal or low in frail or immunosuppressed hosts.
Peripheral neutrophil percentage during bacterial colonic inflammation.
Peripheral absolute neutrophil count.
CRP rises with diverticular inflammation and complicated disease burden.
PCT may rise with severe complicated diverticulitis, bacteremia, or sepsis physiology.
Lactate rises with shock, hypoperfusion, severe sepsis, or bowel catastrophe.
Hemoglobin reflects background anemia, inflammation, bleeding, or dilution rather than diverticulitis-specific injury.
Platelet count may rise with acute inflammation or vary with background disease.
Albumin reflects chronic reserve and acute inflammation; low values raise complication and operative risk context.
Creatinine can rise from dehydration, sepsis, AKI, CKD background, or obstructive ureteral compression from pelvic inflammation.
BUN rises with dehydration, renal dysfunction, GI bleeding, or catabolism.
Hazard of AKI from dehydration, sepsis, shock, contrast, nephrotoxic exposure, or baseline renal vulnerability.
Hazard of macroscopic GI perforation or failure of contained diverticular perforation.
Clinical or imaging evidence of generalized peritonitis from purulent or feculent contamination.
Hazard of septic, hypovolemic, or peritonitis-associated circulatory collapse.
Need for procedural control: percutaneous drainage, operative washout, colectomy/resection, diversion, fistula management, or obstruction relief.
Adequacy of drainage, surgery, diversion, abscess decompression, or nonoperative containment when source control is required.
Persistent uncontrolled perforation, abscess, fistula, obstruction, or sepsis despite attempted management.
Probability that an abscess is large, safely accessible, and drainable by image-guided percutaneous drainage.
Probability that current or candidate antimicrobial regimen covers relevant colonic gram-negative and anaerobic burden at adequate exposure.
Probability that the regimen provides adequate anaerobic colonic flora coverage, especially Bacteroides and mixed abscess flora.
Probability that likely or identified Enterobacterales are susceptible to ceftriaxone or similar third-generation cephalosporin; anaerobic coverage requires a separate lane.
Probability that likely or identified gram-negative colonic flora are susceptible to ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin.
History of severe immediate or severe delayed beta-lactam reaction affecting antibiotic selection.
Need for antimicrobial dose adjustment or toxicity monitoring due to AKI, CKD, dialysis, or nephrotoxic exposure.
Reliability of oral antibiotic absorption and retention, reduced by vomiting, ileus, severe diarrhea, NPO status, shock, or malabsorption.
Global operative risk context from age, frailty, cardiopulmonary disease, coagulopathy, immunosuppression, shock, or poor reserve.

Lifespan mortality hazard for acute diverticulitis emerging from generalized peritonitis, septic shock, AKI, uncontrolled abscess/fistula/obstruction, delayed source control, frailty, and inadequate active coverage.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Sigmoid location drives LLQ pain localization.
Cecal/ascending disease commonly localizes to RLQ.
Hepatic-flexure disease can localize to RUQ.
Wall edema and adjacent fat inflammation often coexist on CT.
Pericolic gas is a direct imaging signal of contained microperforation.
Contained microperforation raises but does not guarantee free perforation risk.
Drainable abscess is a source-control target.
Free air with symptoms increases concern for generalized peritoneal contamination.
Generalized peritonitis requires urgent source-control evaluation.
Adequate drainage, surgery, or containment lowers ongoing source activity.
Uncontrolled abscess, perforation, fistula, or obstruction raises death risk.
Persistent hyperlactatemia signals shock or hypoperfusion.
Fever and pain can raise heart rate, but host factors distort the relationship.
Both often rise with inflammation, though timing and host factors vary.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Supportive care alone does not control drainable abscess, free perforation, obstruction, or fistula.

side_effects.interpretation: Opioid-heavy analgesia can worsen constipation or ileus-like symptoms.

treatments.context_specific_role: Symptom and physiology support while serial exam, labs, and imaging context decide whether antimicrobial or source-control vectors are needed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Gram-negative component needs susceptibility and exposure.
Metronidazole or equivalent anaerobic coverage is needed for mixed colonic flora.
Antibiotics alone may not clear abscess, free perforation, or obstruction.

side_effects.interpretation: Antibiotic-associated diarrhea can overlap colitis mimics.

treatments.context_specific_role: Parenteral active-coverage lane when mixed colonic gram-negative and anaerobic coverage is needed and allergy/resistance context permits.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Vomiting, ileus, NPO status, or shock makes oral exposure unreliable.
Oral therapy alone cannot control free perforation or large abscess.

side_effects.interpretation: GI intolerance or antibiotic-associated diarrhea can occur.

treatments.context_specific_role: Oral active-coverage vector when absorption, stability, and complication/source-control axes support an enteral path.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe systemic physiology increases value of rapid broad active coverage.
Broad antibiotics are not a substitute for drainage or operation.

side_effects.interpretation: Broad-spectrum exposure can cause diarrhea and alter colitis mimic space.

treatments.context_specific_role: Severe or high-risk active-coverage lane while imaging, cultures, and source-control needs are clarified.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage helps only when a safely accessible collection exists.
Incomplete drainage leaves ongoing source activity.

side_effects.interpretation: Bleeding risk depends on access route and coagulopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source-control vector for accessible diverticular abscess; does not replace antibiotics or surgery when generalized peritonitis is active.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Generalized purulent or feculent peritonitis increases value of urgent operation.
Operation helps only if contamination and diseased source are adequately controlled.
Frailty, shock, and comorbidity narrow operative safety margin.

side_effects.interpretation: Operative blood loss and dilution can lower hemoglobin.

treatments.context_specific_role: Operative source-control vector for generalized peritonitis, uncontrolled perforation, obstruction, refractory abscess/fistula, or failure of nonoperative paths.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Known diverticula or prior diverticulitis raises the prior substrate.
Prior disease indicates a susceptible segment.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises prior probability and recurrence context without making the final diagnosis a label.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Frailty raises operative and complication risk.
Older adults may present without fever.
Age and frailty lower reserve for perforation, sepsis, and surgery.

present.trajectory_modulation: Shifts toward atypical presentation and higher outcome hazard.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Immunosuppression increases complicated and perforated disease risk.
Fever, WBC, and CRP response can be muted despite severe disease.
Immunosuppression increases infectious and surgical risk.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises complication hazard while potentially blunting classic inflammatory signs.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Constipation and mucosal injury can amplify diverticular obstruction and inflammation.
Opioids and reduced motility worsen constipation context.
NSAIDs and steroids are associated with complicated diverticular outcomes.

present.trajectory_modulation: Amplifies obstruction/microinjury and complication hazard in susceptible segments.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Comorbidity raises renal and sepsis vulnerability.
CKD/AKI changes antimicrobial dosing and toxicity.
Comorbidity worsens outcomes for the same disease burden.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises organ dysfunction and treatment complexity.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Right-sided substrate shifts expected pain and imaging location.
Right-sided disease often mimics appendicitis with RLQ pain.

present.trajectory_modulation: Shifts localization rather than redefining the first-layer disease leaf.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Inactive or delayed coverage prolongs local burden when antibiotics are needed.
Uncontrolled abscess, perforation, fistula, or obstruction sustains disease.
Persistent source and sepsis raise outcome hazard.

present.trajectory_modulation: Prolongs local and systemic inflammation until active therapy and source control are achieved.

supportive_care: Serial abdominal examination is part of the state trajectory: worsening tenderness, rebound, guarding, distension, fever, tachycardia, hypotension, or lactate should move the posterior toward complicated disease and source-control need.

Use all observed presentation axes rather than a disease-name qualifier: LLQ, RLQ, RUQ, epigastric, cecal, hepatic-flexure, sigmoid, multifocal, abscess, perforation, and immunosuppressed contexts are axes or modifiers.

CT or ultrasound findings should be structured when available: diverticula, inflamed diverticulum, segmental colonic wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, pericolic gas, abscess, pneumoperitoneum, obstruction, and fistula signs.

Keep final pathology, colonoscopy used to adjudicate malignancy/IBD after the acute presentation, operative findings, response to antibiotics, and recurrence/follow-up outcome outside presentation-only ranking unless a post-workup mode explicitly consumes them.

Treat competing mimics fairly: appendicitis, acute cholecystitis/cholangitis, pancreatitis, ischemic or infectious colitis, C. difficile colitis, IBD, gynecologic disease, renal colic/pyelonephritis, malignancy, SBP, and sepsis leaves remain valid when their observed axes are present.
Antibiotic and no-antibiotic decisions should emerge from severity, host risk, abscess/perforation/source-control axes, and RMST simulation, not from a fixed first-line label.

Source control is a state variable: abscess drainage feasibility, source-control adequacy, free perforation, peritonitis, obstruction, and fistula activity determine whether drainage or operation changes the vector field.
quality_notes: Only one derived_hazard axis is present: mortality_hazard_in_D-DIVERTICULITIS.
No direct clinical-decision label fields are used.
New axes are generic reusable ontology candidates for colonic diverticular disease and abdominal imaging, not single-case patches.
